clue.text: Palace supporter disrupted match? No, sir!

indicators.note: something disrupted is thrown out of its usual order, so the letters that follow get rearranged

blocks.note: the letters of these three words, punctuation ignored

explanation.surface: A royal loyalist breaks up a contest, while someone protests to an officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Palace' points to Buckingham Palace, so its supporter backs the Crown.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarchist favours keeping a king or queen, and the palace stands for the royal household.

clue.text: Wizard in match getting swapped, oddly

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters trade places with each other, first with third

blocks.note: a game is a match

explanation.surface: A magician takes part in a contest that gets switched around strangely.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the first and third letters of GAME, the odd ones, to get MAGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A mage is an old or literary word for a magician or sorcerer.

clue.text: Falls over once more — not in rain

indicators.note: turned over, the word for once more is read backwards in a down light
not in tells us to remove the letters of in from the word that follows

blocks.note: again means once more
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something tumbles again, though not out in the rain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Falls' looks like a verb, but it is the waterfall's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Niagara is the famous set of waterfalls on the US–Canada border, so it can be named as Falls.

clue.text: Is it incomprehensible to one unversed in Cockney?

definitions.text: Is it incomprehensible to one unversed in Cockney?

blocks.clueFragment: Is it incomprehensible to one unversed in Cockney?
blocks.note: surface reading: is London dialect hard to follow for an outsider
setter's reading: one with no knowledge of the verses, the paired rhymes that replace ordinary words in East End speech

explanation.walkthrough: 'Unversed' means unfamiliar, but also hints at verse and rhyme: the Cockney code swaps words for rhyming phrases, like apples and pears for stairs.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyming slang is the Cockney practice of replacing a word with a phrase that rhymes with it, often baffling outsiders.

clue.text: I'm taking a risk in present travels

blocks.note: here means present, as when answering a register
goes means travels

explanation.surface: Someone gambling on a current journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' looks like a gift, but it means in attendance.
explanation.definitionFit: Here goes is a spoken idiom said just before attempting something daring or uncertain.

clue.text: Tiny piece of money I exchanged with pound

indicators.note: one named letter trades places with the abbreviation for a pound, a minimal rearrangement within the word

blocks.note: silver is coins, loose change

explanation.surface: A small coin changed for a pound.
explanation.walkthrough: Pound is L, from Latin libra; in SILVER swap the I with the L to get SLIVER.
explanation.definitionFit: A sliver is a very small, thin piece of something, such as a sliver of cake or glass.

clue.text: Soft edge receives mark

indicators.note: to receive something is to take it inside, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: a lip is the rim or edge of a cup or crater
M is the abbreviation for the old German currency, the mark

explanation.surface: A soft border takes on a stain or scratch.
explanation.definitionFit: Limp describes something floppy and lacking stiffness, close in meaning to soft.

clue.text: Elementary form is to put in work on English

indicators.note: to put something in is to insert it inside another word

blocks.note: taken as written
op is short for opus, a work
taken as written
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Something basic needs to be applied to English work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elementary' means a form of a chemical element, not something simple.
explanation.definitionFit: An isotope is one of several forms of a chemical element differing in neutron count.

clue.text: In history, it's simple to revise a previously used paper

indicators.note: in places the following material inside the word for history
revising something means reworking it, so these letters are reordered

blocks.note: the past is history
taken as written

explanation.surface: A historian says it is easy to rewrite the record.
explanation.walkthrough: The shuffled letters of simple go inside PAST, between its A and S.
explanation.definitionFit: A palimpsest is a manuscript scraped clean and written over again, so the page was used before.

clue.text: Having the sauce to aim for source of easy money

blocks.note: gravy is a meat sauce
to train a gun is to aim it

explanation.surface: Someone has the cheek to go after easy cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having the sauce' suggests cheek, as sauce also means impudence; here it is simply the meat sauce.
explanation.definitionFit: A gravy train is an idiom for a job or scheme yielding large profits for little effort.

clue.text: Parrot's head

blocks.note: first meaning: read as 'Parrot is', the stock pet name for a parrot, as in Pretty Polly
second meaning: an old word for the top of the head

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one bird's head; the 's is really 'is', so the clue says a parrot is a head.
explanation.definitionFit: Poll is a stock name for a pet parrot, and also an archaic word for the scalp or crown of a person.

clue.text: Rest of burial party's job?

blocks.note: to inter is to bury
a mission is a task assigned to a group

explanation.surface: What's left of the work of a funeral group.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as one phrase, the job of a burial party is an inter-mission.
explanation.definitionFit: An intermission is a break or pause in a performance, a time to rest.

clue.text: With arid spell, possibly, river disappears here

definitions.text: With arid spell, possibly, river disappears here

indicators.note: a spell of letters is one possible spelling, so another arrangement of them is wanted
whatever disappears is lost from the word it was in

blocks.note: W is the standard abbreviation for with
taken as written
R is the map abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: In a dry spell a river vanishes into the ground at this place.
explanation.walkthrough: Take R out of ARID and rearrange the rest after W to get WADI; the whole clue also describes one.
explanation.definitionFit: A wadi is a desert valley whose stream runs only after rain and dries away in arid seasons.

clue.text: Space on grassy area that's provided for players to relax

definitions.text: that's provided for players to relax

blocks.note: a green is a grassy area such as a village green
room means space, as in room to move

explanation.surface: A lawn somewhere has a spot set aside for athletes to unwind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' places the space after the grassy area. 'Players' sounds sporting but means actors.
explanation.definitionFit: A green room is the lounge in a theatre where performers wait and rest before going on stage.

clue.text: Grimes's profits in gambling enterprise

blocks.note: Mr Grimes is the chimney sweep in Kingsley's The Water Babies
the take is the money earned

explanation.surface: A man called Grimes makes money in a betting venture.
explanation.walkthrough: Grimes is the cruel chimney sweep in Charles Kingsley's children's novel The Water Babies.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweepstake is a lottery-style bet where all the stakes are pooled and paid to the winners.

clue.text: One would dispute his degree was top-class

blocks.note: first meaning: someone who wrangles, an arguer
second meaning: a Cambridge student gaining first-class honours in mathematics

explanation.walkthrough: At Cambridge University, anyone with a first in the maths degree is called a wrangler.
explanation.definitionFit: To wrangle is to argue, so a wrangler is a debater; the word is also a Cambridge title for top mathematics graduates.

clue.text: Parts of river finally reversing direction

indicators.note: the closing letter is a compass point that turns round to face the opposite way

blocks.note: the Severn is Britain's longest river

explanation.surface: Stretches of a river at last flow back the other way.
explanation.walkthrough: SEVERN ends in N for north; reverse that direction to S for south and you get SEVERS.
explanation.definitionFit: To sever is to cut apart or separate, the same as the verb parts.

clue.text: Drawing fuel

blocks.note: first meaning: a sketch made with a charred stick
second meaning: the carbon used on barbecues

explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawing fuel' suggests sucking up petrol; the words are two separate senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Charcoal names both an artist's sketch done in burnt wood and the carbon that burns on a barbecue.

clue.text: Puff away, being no longer fit?

blocks.note: ex means former, no longer what it was
hale means healthy and fit

explanation.surface: Someone out of shape gasps for breath.
explanation.walkthrough: An ex-hale person is one no longer fit, a whimsical reading of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: To exhale is to breathe out, which is what a puff of breath does.

clue.text: Making slow progress, not liking to cross line

indicators.note: a word crossing something spans it, so it holds the line inside

blocks.note: hating is the opposite of liking
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: Someone shuffling along, reluctant to step over a mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Halting means hesitant and faltering, moving forward only with difficulty and pauses.

clue.text: Dictionary used by judge

blocks.note: first meaning: the Edinburgh-published dictionary long favoured by crossword setters
second meaning: a judge's private rooms where cases are heard out of court

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a judge consulting a dictionary; the second half is the judge's office.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers is a well-known British dictionary publisher, and also the term for a judge's private offices.

clue.text: Pull out from tour heartlessly, being in demand

indicators.note: without its heart the word loses its middle, leaving only the outside letters
being in something means sitting inside it

blocks.note: to exact is to demand
just the first and last letters

explanation.surface: Someone withdraws from a trip coldly, being much sought after.
explanation.definitionFit: To extract is to draw or pull something out, as a dentist does a tooth.

clue.text: Foresee a holding in good wine-bar

indicators.note: holding something in means keeping it inside

blocks.note: to bode is to foretell or portend
taken as written
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Someone predicts a decent taverna will hold its own.
explanation.walkthrough: BODE A holds G between its parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Bodega is the Spanish term for a cellar or shop selling drink, borrowed into English for such a bar.

clue.text: Gone off to capture place - aim for glory

indicators.note: capturing something means taking it and holding it inside

blocks.note: milk that has gone off has turned sour
PL is the abbreviation for place, as in street names
an end is a goal or aim

explanation.surface: A soldier leaves to seize a position, chasing military honour.
explanation.definitionFit: Splendour is magnificent brilliance or grandeur, which is what glory means here.

clue.text: Plot reported a good deal

indicators.note: a report is spoken, so we want a word heard rather than written

blocks.note: a sight more means a good deal more

explanation.surface: A news item tells of a bargain over a scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plot' looks like a scheme, but it is a piece of land.
explanation.definitionFit: A site is a plot of land on which something is or will be built.

clue.text: Vital passage some have infiltrated

indicators.note: some means only part of the following words is taken

blocks.note: spans the end of one word and start of the next

explanation.surface: Some people have got into an important corridor.
explanation.definitionFit: A vein is a blood vessel, a channel the body cannot live without.

clue.text: As some say, opposed to a machine

blocks.note: taken as written
a gin is a machine, as in the cotton gin

explanation.surface: Some people say they are against machinery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As some say' marks a dialect word, not a sound-alike: agin is a rural form of against.
explanation.definitionFit: Agin is a dialect or folksy form of against, meaning hostile toward or set against something.

clue.text: Mentioned a different name

indicators.note: a different version of the letters is a new arrangement of them

blocks.note: the letters of both words

explanation.surface: Someone referred to an alternative title.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mentioned' looks like the definition, being a verb in the past, but it is fodder; the definition is the final word.
explanation.definitionFit: To denominate is to give something a title or designation, a formal synonym for the verb name.

clue.text: Privet for example, commonly said to be used for boundary

indicators.note: common speech here means a dropped initial h, so we listen to a casual pronunciation

blocks.note: privet is a shrub grown as a garden hedge, said here with the h dropped

explanation.surface: Privet is usually planted to mark where a garden ends.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping the h is the classic Cockney or 'common' pronunciation.
explanation.definitionFit: An edge is the outer limit or border of an area, the same as a boundary.

clue.text: Not returning to delightful Northern town

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so the word not is read backwards

blocks.note: darling as an adjective means charming or delightful
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to go back to a charming town in the north.
explanation.walkthrough: Darlington is a town in County Durham, north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Darlington is a market town in the north of England, famous for the early Stockton and Darlington Railway.
